```{r setup}
library(DLNMLPS)
```


# Introduction

Classical distributed lag non-linear models (DLNMs) assume a common exposure-lag-response relationships across geographical areas. However, this relationship might be altered by an effect modifier that differs between spatial units. For example, the relationship between temperature and mortality may differ between regions according to the deprivation index.

`DLNMLPS` provides methods for fitting effect-modified distributed lag non-linear models, allowing the exposure-lag-response relationship to vary according to a continuous or categorical covariate [@Rutten2026confounding]. This framework allows for flexible interactions between the DLNM and a possibly non-linear smooth covariate.

In this vignette, we demonstrate how to fit covariate-varying DLNMs using `DLNMLPS` and show how to predict and visualize the exposure-lag-response relationship.

The basic functionality of `DLNMLPS`is introduced in `vignette("introduction_dlnmlps")`.

# Effect-modified DLNMs

## Example data
For illustration, we use the following simulated example data:

```{r}
# Example data
data(barcelona_temp)
```

This simulated data set contains daily minimum, maximum and mean temperature in all 10 districts of Barcelona during the summer period (1 June--30 September) between 2007 and 2011. The population size, deprivation index and daily number of deaths are included for every district. For this example, we will investigate how the effect of maximum temperature on mortality spatially varies according to the deprivation index. The outcome and exposure variable can then be inspected:

```{r}
# Inspect the data
head(barcelona_temp)
```

We can extract some additional information from the date such as the day of the week, year and month.
```{r}
# Extract date information
dataset <- barcelona_temp |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    dow = weekdays(date),
    year = lubridate::year(date),
    month = lubridate::month(date)
  )
```

## Fitting an effect-modified DLNM
The `DLNMLPS` package provides a lot of flexibility in modelling effect modification. In this example, we will fit four different models:

- **Categorical effect modification**, a penalized DLNM modified by a categorical deprivation index;

- **Linear effect modification**, a penalized DLNM modified by a continuous deprivation index, using a linear interaction;

- **Smooth unpenalized effect modification**, a penalized DLNM modified by a continuous deprivation index, expressed by natural splines using 2 knots (on the 10% and 90% percentile);

- **Smooth penalized effect modification**, a penalized DLNM modified by a continuous deprivation index, expressed by penalized splines using 5 df.

We include month as natural splines with 3 degrees of freedom, year as a random walk of order one, day of the week as a factor and District as an independent random effect. We use a penalized DLNM with 8 degrees of freedom and penalty of order 2.

For the first model, we split the deprivation index in a categorical variable with three levels. We specify the modifying covariate through the option `by` and include `type`="factor" in the argument `arg.by`. We also include the categorical deprivation index as a main effect in the model. The model can be fitted as:

```{r}
# Fit a categorical modified DLNM
group <- factor(paste0(dataset$District, "-", dataset$year))

basis.max_pen <- dlnm::crossbasis(
  dataset$Tmax,
  argvar = list(fun = "ps", df = 8),
  arglag = list(fun = "ps", df = 8),
  lag = 14,
  group = group
)

dataset$depriv_cat <- ifelse(dataset$depriv <= quantile(dataset$depriv,0.25), "low",
                             ifelse(dataset$depriv >= quantile(dataset$depriv,0.75), "high", "medium"))

model1 <- DLNM_LPS(dtot ~ factor(dow) + factor(depriv_cat) +
                        sm(basis.max_pen, arg = list(pen = 2),
                           by = depriv_cat, arg.by = list(type = "factor")) +
                        sm(month, arg = list(type = "ns", df = 3)) +
                        sm(year, arg = list(type = "rw1")) +
                        sm(District, arg = list(type = "ind")),
                   data = dataset,
                   offset = log(pop),
                   model.comparison = list(DIC = TRUE, WAIC = TRUE, CPO = TRUE),
                   family = "Poisson")

```

The second model can similarly be fitted by specifying `type`="linear" instead of `type`="factor". Deprivation index is now also included as a linear main effect:

```{r}
# Fit a linear modified DLNM
model2 <- DLNM_LPS(dtot ~ factor(dow) + depriv +
                        sm(basis.max_pen, arg = list(pen = 2),
                           by = depriv, arg.by = list(type = "linear")) +
                        sm(month, arg = list(type = "ns", df = 3)) +
                        sm(year, arg = list(type = "rw1")) +
                        sm(District, arg = list(type = "ind")),
                   data = dataset,
                   offset = log(pop),
                   model.comparison = list(DIC = TRUE, WAIC = TRUE, CPO = TRUE),
                   family = "Poisson")

```

For the third model, we include deprivation index as a smooth effect, using natural splines with two knots. The model can be fitted as:

```{r}
# Fit an unpenalized smooth modified DLNM
knots_depriv <- quantile(dataset$depriv, probs = c(0.10,0.90))

model3 <- DLNM_LPS(dtot ~ factor(dow) + sm(depriv, arg = list(type = "ns", knots = knots_depriv)) +
                        sm(basis.max_pen, arg = list(pen = 2),
                           by = depriv, arg.by = list(type = "ns", knots = knots_depriv)) +
                        sm(month, arg = list(type = "ns", df = 3)) +
                        sm(year, arg = list(type = "rw1")) +
                        sm(District, arg = list(type = "ind")),
                   data = dataset,
                   offset = log(pop),
                   model.comparison = list(DIC = TRUE, WAIC = TRUE, CPO = TRUE),
                   family = "Poisson")

```

Lastly, in the fourth model, we include an interaction with deprivation index using penalized splines:

```{r}
# Fit an penalized smooth modified DLNM
model4 <- DLNM_LPS(dtot ~ factor(dow) + sm(depriv, arg = list(type = "ps", df = 5, pen = 2)) +
                        sm(basis.max_pen, arg = list(pen = 2),
                           by = depriv, arg.by = list(type = "ps", df = 5, pen = 2)) +
                        sm(month, arg = list(type = "ns", df = 3)) +
                        sm(year, arg = list(type = "rw1")) +
                        sm(District, arg = list(type = "ind")),
                   data = dataset,
                   offset = log(pop),
                   model.comparison = list(DIC = TRUE, WAIC = TRUE, CPO = TRUE),
                   family = "Poisson")

```

We can compare the performance of the four models using model comparison criteria DIC, WAIC and CPO:

```{r}
# Compare the estimated associations
model1$DIC; model1$WAIC; -sum(log(model1$CPO))
model2$DIC; model2$WAIC; -sum(log(model2$CPO))
model3$DIC; model3$WAIC; -sum(log(model3$CPO))
model4$DIC; model4$WAIC; -sum(log(model4$CPO))
```

The fourth model is preferred based on all model selection criteria. Using this model, we predict the exposure-lag-response curve for three different levels of the deprivation index (2.5%, 50% and 97.5%) at temperatures between 22 and 30 degrees Celsius, relative to a centering value of 25 degrees. We also request the probability that the logarithm of the relative risk exceeds 0:

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
pred_penalized <- pred_crossbasis(
  basis = basis.max_pen,
  model = model4,
  at_x = seq(22,30,length = 50),
  cen = 25,
  lag = c(0,14),
  CI = TRUE,
  by = round(quantile(dataset$depriv, probs = c(0.025,0.50,0.975)),2),
  exc.prob = TRUE
)
```

Using the `extract_predictions()` function, we can easily extract (part of) the requested predictions. For example, if interest is in the lag-specific RR for lag 0 and lag 2 at 22 and 30 degrees and for deprivation quantiles 2.5% and 97.5%, we can use:

```{r}
extract_predictions(pred_penalized, slice_x = c(22,30), slice_lag = c(0,2), 
                    slice_by = round(quantile(dataset$depriv, probs = c(0.025,0.975)),2), 
                    ptype = "matRRfit")
```


To plot the exposure-response relationship at lag 0, 3 and 8 for the 2.5%, 50% and 97.5% percentile deprivation indices, we can use:

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
plot(pred_penalized, slice_lag = c(0,3,8), ptype = "slices", CI = TRUE, 
     xlab = "temperature", ylab = "RR")
```

Based on this plot, the differences in temporal evolution of the RR, based on deprivation index, seem to be small. The plot title indicates the level of deprivation. The option `multiple.plots` = FALSE allows visualizing the results for different levels of the deprivation index on one plot. Note that this option is only available for an integer (and not a vector) slice value or overall RR-curve. Furthermore, the option `slice_by` allows to specify only a subset of the predicted `by`-values. For example, if we only want to plot the 2.5% and 97.5% deprivation percentiles, we can use:

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
plot(pred_penalized, slice_x = 30, 
     slice_by = round(quantile(dataset$depriv,probs = c(0.025,0.975)),2), 
     ptype = "slices", CI = TRUE, xlab = "lag", ylab = "RR", multiple.plots = FALSE)
plot(pred_penalized, slice_by = round(quantile(dataset$depriv, probs = c(0.025,0.975)),2), 
     ptype = "overall", CI = TRUE, xlab = "temperature", ylab = "RR",  
     multiple.plots = FALSE)
```

At high temperatures, there is some evidence that the overall RR is lower for municipalities with a low deprivation index. A contour plot of the exposure-lag-response relationship can also be made for different deprivation levels:

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
contour(pred_penalized, ptype = "cross", xlab = "lag", ylab = "temperature")
```

# Summary

In this vignette, we introduced the effect modifying functionality of `DLNMLPS`. We demonstrated how to fit four different models, differing in the flexibility of the effect modification. We used penalized splines to showcase the functionality of the package but similar models can be fitted with unpenalized splines. See also `vignette("introduction_dlnmlps")` for more information.
